body:
Dear Sir,



This is to provide an update on the successful completion of the department demonstration for the Compensation and Elephant Transit modules to the Wildlife Section.

Demonstrated the Public Entry option with Mobile Number OTP-based registration with Multilingual support.

Explained all fields in the three-step application form.

Demonstrated the complete workflows separately for Human Death, Human Injury, Crop Damage, Property Damage, and Cattle Death/Injury compensation categories.

Explained the complete Range Officer workflow, including all available features after application submission.

Demonstrated the DFO workflow along with all processing features.

Explained the Circle Office workflow for Human Death cases, including forwarding the application to the DFO for settlement.

dated 28.12.2023

15.12.2025
*****
I submit that in the reference 2nd cited above the District Forest Officer
Gudalur Division has stated that, as per the Government Order G.O. (Ms) No. 233, Environment,
Climate Change and Forests Department, dated 28.12.2023, administrative sanction has been
accorded for a sum of Rs. 6.00 crore for the establishment of a Command-and-Control Centre to
strengthen the management of Human Wildlife Conflict in prioritized and high-conflict areas of the
Gudalur Forest Division. This initiative marks a significant step towards adopting advanced,
technology-driven approaches to safeguard human life, protect wildlife, and promote coexistence
in a landscape where conventional mitigation measures alone have proved inadequate.
The proposed Command-and-Control Centre building at Gene pool Garden will
function as a dedicated operational hub for integrating advanced surveillance technologies and
coordinating all Human Wildlife Conflict management activities. The project includes the
deployment of 46 AI-enabled camera systems, comprising twelve multi-sensor tower cameras
equipped with visible, RADAR, and thermal imaging capabilities, twenty-four alert stations, one
hub station, and one repeater station.
The Command-and-Control Centre will operate as a centralised platform for
continuous surveillance, real-time data integration, early warning dissemination, and coordinated
field response. By monitoring critical elephant movement corridors and sensitive locations across
the division, the system will generate instant alerts to field staff, local communities, and other
stakeholders, thereby enabling timely interventions to prevent conflict situations.
For the effective functioning of the Command-and-Control Centre, a robust
institutional framework supported by a trained operations team and clearly defined Standard
Operating Procedures (SOP) is hereby required. The SOP for field response to Wildlife Movement
Alerts and Human–Wildlife Conflict Mitigation, as well as SOP for the Operation and Management
of the Command-and-Control Centre (CCC) have been developed. Further, the District Forest
Officer has requested to approve the Standard Operating Procedure.
I request that the District Forest Officer request for approval of SOP may kindly
approved, so as to enable the smooth and effective operationalisation of the Command-and-
Control Centre in the Gudalur Forest Division.
Encl As. above Yours faithfully
KIRUBASHANKKAR R

Flash Reports Workflow changes
We need to do the following changes in flash reports
Form Changes:
1. Need to add a new field “Inside / Outside RF”
2. If user choose inside RF, then we need to collect “Reserve Forest Name”
Human Injury / Death:
1. In Human death and injury we need to follow the below work flow
FRO – Data entry and submit, system will forward that to DFO. DFO will get notification.
DFO – After DFO approval, Flash report will be sent to
a. PCCF HOFF – by mail and portal notification
b. CWLW – by mail and portal notification
c. WL Section logins – Portal notification only
d. CF/CCF - by Portal notification only
WL Section – Section can send mail to Government only for Human Death
Following Mail ids will be configured by WL Section
Animal Injury/ Death:
1. Animan injury to be removed and animal flash report type can be modified as
radio button. Also rename the title as “Animal Death”
2. Report type options:
a. Options : Elephant, Tiger, Leopard, Other Schedule-I Animals(Ref Master)
3. If user selected Other Schedule-I animal, then collect “Animal Name” Instead of
type of animal. Type of animal field should be removed.
Elephant Death Workflow:
FRO – Data entry and submit, system will forward that to DFO. DFO will get notification.
DFO – After DFO approval, Flash report will be sent to
a. PCCF HOFF – by mail and portal notification
b. CWLW – by mail and portal notification
c. WL Section logins – Portal notification only
d. CF/CCF - by Portal notification only
e. Government – by Mail only
f. Minister Office – by Mail only
Leopard and Tiger Death Workflow:
FRO – Data entry and submit, system will forward that to DFO. DFO will get notification.
DFO – After DFO approval, Flash report will be sent to
a. PCCF HOFF – by mail and portal notification
b. CWLW – by mail and portal notification
c. WL Section logins – Portal notification only
d. CF/CCF - by Portal notification only
e. Government – by Mail only
f. Minister Office – by Mail only
Schedul-I Animal Death Workflow:
FRO – Data entry and submit, system will forward that to DFO. DFO will get notification.
DFO – After DFO approval, Flash report will be sent to
a. PCCF HOFF – by mail and portal notification
b. CWLW – by mail and portal notification
c. WL Section logins – Portal notification only
d. CF/CCF - by Portal notification only
Mail Format:
Need to design a mail template for flash report and that to be shared with respective
officials.
Schedule-I Animal Master:
Bear, Byson, Crocodile, Deer, Snake, Lion-tailed Macaque, Nilgiri Tahr, Indian Pangolin,
Nilgiri Langur, Grizzled Giant Squirrel, Smooth-coated Otter

Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham— ForestGuard | Tamil Nadu Forest Department - Innovative Project Proposal
2026
INNOVATIVE PROJECT PROPOSAL
Submitted by
Dr. M Senthilkumar, Professor, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore
Dr. K. Baranidharan, Professor, TNAU Forest College & Research Institute, Coimbatore
Dr C Bagavathi, Assistant Professor, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore
Dr J Uma, Assistant Professor, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore
ForestGuard: AI-Enabled Multi-Scale Forest
Disturbance and Human–Wildlife Conflict Risk
Prediction System for Proactive Landscape
Management
Project Category: MIS and AI Intervention in Management of Forests & Wildlife
Project Title ForestGuard: AI-Enabled Multi-Scale Forest Disturbance and
Human–Wildlife Conflict Risk Prediction System for Proactive
Landscape Management
Project Category MIS and AI Intervention in Management of Forests & Wildlife
Proponent Institution Amrita School of Computing, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore
Principal Investigator Dr. M Senthilkumar, Professor, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore
Dr. K. Baranidharan, Professor, TNAU Forest College & Research Institute, CBE
Dr C Bagavathi, Assistant Professor, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore
Dr J Uma, Assistant Professor, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore
Project Duration 24 Months
Estimated Budget INR 26,50,000 (Rupees Twenty-Six Lakhs and Fifty Thousand Only)
Submission Date July 15, 2026
1. Executive Summary
Human–wildlife conflict is an ongoing problem in the environment, which is caused by degradation of forests,
fragmentation of habitat, expansion of agriculture, construction of infrastructure and disturbances of wildlife
movement. Most mitigation efforts are reactive, in that they only take place after crop loss, destruction of property,
livestock predation, or human injury has already occurred [1]. This project aims to develop an integrated AI-based
approach for early conflict prediction that integrates satellite remote sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS),
machine learning, IoT-based wildlife sensing and social vulnerability assessment. Google Earth Engine processing
of sentinel-1 and sentinel-2 satellite imagery will be used to identify forest disturbance, habitat fragmentation and
encroachment [2]. These indicators will be linked to past human-wildlife conflict incidents to see if there are
environmental changes that precede the conflict events. Prediction models will be built species by species with
Random Forest, XGBoost and Convolutional Neural Networks for the main groups of conflict species such as
megaherbivores, large carnivores, primates and venomous reptiles. The occurrence data of the wildlife gathered by
Mettupalayam Forest Division will be combined with the GIS-based environmental layers. A Social Vulnerability
Index will be developed based on socio-economic, land-use, crop and community data to estimate the severity of
conflict. This will create a hierarchical early-warning system, which will combine wildlife detection, conflict-risk
prediction and vulnerability mapping. It will be tested with the Forest Department and local communities and provide
an open-source dashboard, AI models, risk maps, deployment guidelines, and policy recommendations.
Project Duration: 24 Months | Estimated Budget: INR 26,50,000
2. Background and Problem Statement
The issue of human–wildlife conflict has become a significant ecological, social and governance problem in
forest-fringe areas. Habitat fragmentation, degradation of forests, linear infrastructure development, agriculture
expansion, invasive vegetation [4], water scarcity and decreased connectivity between forest patches are changing
the way wildlife moves. Wildlife species are increasingly entering into agricultural fields, villages, livestock areas,
roads, peri-urban settlements in search of food, water, shelter and corridors for movement.
Page 1 | 4
Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham— ForestGuard | Tamil Nadu Forest Department - Innovative Project Proposal
2026
The repercussions are dire. Crop damage, loss of livestock, property destruction, injuries, fear and economic
insecurity are all observed in communities. Forest departments are under greater pressure to respond quickly to
incidents and are also responsible for managing wildlife conservation, habitat restoration and public safety. The
existing conflict response systems typically rely on complaints registers, patrol reports, compensation claims and
post-incident field visits. These are the approaches that are reactive and are important. They are not a good predictor
of the location of conflict, the communities at greatest risk, or the role of forest disturbance in future conflict risk.
Satellite remote sensing provides an opportunity to monitor forest disturbance, vegetation loss, crop expansion, water
availability, and habitat fragmentation at large spatial scales. However, forest-change data are rarely integrated with
conflict incident databases in an operational predictive framework. Similarly, camera traps and acoustic sensors can
detect wildlife locally, but their outputs are typically not linked to landscape-scale risk prediction models. There is
also limited incorporation of social vulnerability into conflict-risk mapping [3]. A conflict event in a highly vulnerable
village may have much greater social and economic consequences than a similar event in a better-resourced settlement
[5]. The above context clearly conveys that the human-wildlife conflict incidents are escalating across forest fringe
areas, and this costs human lives and penalizes the livelihoods, yet the existing monitoring and mitigation efforts
remain reactive, fragmented, and unable to anticipate the risk before such incidents occur. Thus, the core problem is
the absence of an integrated, near-real-time, multi-scale, and socially informed early-warning system that can predict
human–wildlife conflict risk before incidents. This project addresses this gap by combining satellite-based forest
disturbance monitoring, AI-based species-specific risk prediction, IoT-based field sensing, and community
vulnerability mapping into a unified decision-support platform.
3. Objectives
O1: To design a near real-time forest monitoring framework that links satellite-derived forest disturbance with
conflict incident data.
O2: To build, train and validate an intelligent conflict risk prediction method for multi-species groups includes mega
herbivorous, large carnivorous and venomous reptiles.
O3: To integrate IoT-based field sensors with GIS-based risk models, creating a hierarchical alert system from
individual wildlife detections to zone-level risk warnings.
O4: To construct a Social Vulnerability Index by integrating socioeconomic indicators, land tenure, crop type,
settlement characteristics, and attitudinal survey data to incorporate it into conflict-impact severity mapping.
O5: To test and validate the integrated system with forest department personnel and local community representatives
in two pilot landscapes and develop an open-source dashboard for scalable deployment.
4. Methodology
Phase Description
4.1 Study Area Select two pilot forest-fringe landscapes with stakeholder engagement,
Selection focusing on ecological and conflict contexts. Initial meetings will identify
priority species, reporting systems, and operational needs.
4.2 Data Develop an integrated spatial database with layers including historical
Collection conflict incidents, wildlife sightings, land-use maps, socioeconomic
indicators, and community surveys.
4.3 Forest Use Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery for near-real-time detection of
Change forest cover loss, vegetation stress, and habitat fragmentation. Map
Detection disturbance events linked to conflict records.
4.4 Conflict- Create models for different conflict guilds using machine learning
Risk Prediction techniques (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost) to evaluate predictors like
forest disturbance and historical conflict frequency.
4.5 IoT Install detection nodes at high-risk locations equipped with cameras,
Detection acoustic sensors, and edge AI for wildlife detection. Transmit data to the
Nodes central database to update risk scores.
4.6 Alert Develop a three-level alert system based on wildlife detection, risk
System probability, and social vulnerability, prioritizing alerts with a combined
risk score.
Page 2 | 4
Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham— ForestGuard | Tamil Nadu Forest Department - Innovative Project Proposal
2026
5. Innovation and Novelty
1. Integrated forest disturbance–conflict modelling: The project moves beyond static conflict maps by
explicitly modelling how forest disturbance events precede conflict escalation.
2. Multi-species and multi-guild AI prediction: Instead of treating all human–wildlife conflict as one
category, the project develops species-sensitive risk models for ecologically distinct wildlife groups.
3. Hierarchical sensing architecture: The system integrates satellite-scale monitoring, GIS-based risk
prediction, and field-level IoT sensing.
4. Socially informed conflict prediction: The Social Vulnerability Index ensures that the system predicts not
only where wildlife may enter human-use areas, but also where conflict impacts may be most severe.
5. Spatially robust AI validation: Spatially blocked train-test protocols will improve the scientific credibility
and real-world transferability of the prediction models.
6. Operational early-warning dashboard: The final system will be designed as a decision-support platform
for forest officers rather than only as a research prototype.
7. Open-source and replicable design: The platform, models, data schemas, and deployment protocols will
be structured for adaptation across forest divisions and states.
6. Project Outcomes and Expected Impact
1. Forest disturbance detection near real time pipeline based on Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2 and Google Earth
Engine.
2. Geospatial database that incorporates forest change, presence of wildlife, conflict incidents, socioeconomic
indicators and field sensor data.
3. AI models for predicting conflict risk for each species in each wildlife guild.
4. Spatially validated conflict hotspot maps and seasonal risk maps.
5. Wildlife detection nodes with edge-based inference capability powered by the Internet of Things (IoT).
6. Hierarchical alert system: combining point level detection, zone level risk and social vulnerability.
7. Maps of social vulnerability and the severity of the conflict.
8. Open-source decision support dashboard for forest departments.
9. Two pilot landscapes deployed and tested their deployment protocol.
10. At least three good journal publications, one technical manual and one open-source software repository.
